newsitem.title: UK: Arsonists attack Northern Ireland church.
newsitem.headline: Arsonists attack Northern Ireland church.

text.p: A Protestant church was set ablaze in a Roman Catholic section of Northern Ireland's second city on Friday in continued tension between extremists from the two communities.
Arsonists broke into the 160-year-old building and used flammable liquid to start a blaze that burned out the vestry, destroyed a century-old organ and wrecked the roof.

"I have no doubt that I am speaking for the mass of the people of this city in both sections of our community in the utter condemnation of the people who carried this out," said Nobel Peace Prize nominee John Hume.

"I hope this is not part of an orchestrated campaign against Protestants in this city. I wouldn't understand anyone in any position of responsibility who would want to organise a campaign of this nature," said Hume, leader of the Catholic-backed Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP).
It was the second attack against the Church of Ireland's Christ Church in four weeks and followed a series of incidents in which Protestant and Catholic targets have been hit across the province.
"I feel sorry for people who get kicks out of setting fire to a church," said Canon Donald McClean.

Tension has been running high in Northern Ireland since sectarian violence flared in the summer when Protestants paralysed the province with demonstrations to secure permission for a traditional Orange Order parade in a Catholic area.
Catholics and Protestants have boycotted each others' shops in various parts of Northern Ireland and several churches of both faiths have been vandalised or picketed.
By its own bloody standards Northern Ireland is enjoying a period of relative peace because of the absence of guerrilla campaigns by pro-Irish IRA and pro-British Loyalist gunmen.
But barely a day passes without extremists attacking a target on the rival side of the sectarian divide.
Church leaders say the failure of Anglo-Irish peace talks to make even a start on a political settlement is undermining popular confidence in the peace process.
The talks, chaired by former Senator George Mitchell. have not held a full, opening plenary session since they started in June.
